hero.name: Lakshmi
hero.who: a 43-year-old homemaker in Coimbatore who dreams of selling her homemade podi

story.b: Lakshmi's podis are famous in her apartment block in Saibaba Colony. Paruppu podi, curry leaf podi, and the fiery idli podi her late mother taught her. Neighbours often joke that she should sell them. Now that her son has left for college in Chennai, she wants to try. Her husband's friend, who runs a printing business, has big plans for her. Rent a small shop, buy a commercial grinder, print two thousand branded boxes, open a website. He adds it all up on a paper napkin at Sunday lunch: nearly three lakh rupees. Lakshmi's stomach tightens. That is most of their savings. She believes in her podi, but she has no idea whether strangers will actually pay for it.

ask.q: Lakshmi is told to spend three lakh rupees on a shop and boxes before selling anything. What should she think about first?
o: Whether strangers will really pay for her podi, before spending big
Which shop location has the most people walking past
How to design the most attractive box so it sells itself
ask.why: Her whole plan rests on an untested guess that strangers will buy. Choosing a location or a box design assumes that guess is already true. Finding out whether people will pay comes first, because it decides whether any of the big spending makes sense.

chapters.take: Before spending big on an idea, find out if people actually want it.

story.b: Lakshmi takes out her son's old school notebook and writes at the top: my guesses. Strangers will pay one hundred and twenty rupees for a two-hundred-gram packet. They will like the taste enough to come back. Office workers will want it most. Writing them down, she realises how little she actually knows. Every line is a guess dressed up as a fact. Her neighbour Meena says she is overthinking it, since everyone already loves her podi. But everyone means friends who get it free. Lakshmi circles the first guess. If strangers will not pay, nothing else matters. She decides to test it before spending more than a few hundred rupees on anything.

ask.q: Lakshmi has written several guesses about her business. Which should she test first?
o: Whether office workers are the best customers
Whether strangers will actually pay her price
Whether a website or an app would work better
ask.why: A plan is a set of guesses, and the riskiest one is the guess everything else depends on. If strangers will not pay, the customer group and the website do not matter. Testing that first, cheaply, tells her whether to go further at all.

chapters.take: Treat your plan as a set of guesses, and test the riskiest one first.

story.h: Forty packets at the Sunday market
story.b: Lakshmi's friend Selvi has a stall at a Sunday organic market near Race Course, and she offers Lakshmi one corner of her table. Lakshmi makes forty small packets, a few of each podi, writes prices on a piece of cardboard and keeps a notebook ready. She tallies every sale and every comment. Idli podi sells out by ten. Curry leaf podi sells slowly. Three customers say the packets are too big to try a new flavour. That evening she changes three things: more idli podi, smaller trial packets, and a sample spoon for tasting. The next Sunday she sells almost everything. She now has a simple rhythm: make a little, watch closely, change one thing, repeat.

ask.q: After her first Sunday, Lakshmi has a notebook full of sales and comments. What should she do next?
o: Ignore the comments and make exactly the same batch again
Stop and spend a month perfecting every recipe before returning
Make small changes based on what she saw and test again next Sunday
ask.why: The point of a small test is to learn fast. Using what she saw to adjust and test again turns each week into a lesson. Repeating the same batch wastes what she learned, and a month of perfecting in the kitchen means a month without real customers.

chapters.take: Build a little, watch what people do, learn and go again, quickly.

story.b: Customers start asking if they can order on weekdays. Lakshmi's son Karthik, home for the holidays, is excited. He wants to build a proper website with a shopping cart, and says it will take two months and around forty thousand rupees. Lakshmi asks what the simplest version could be. Together they make a single photo of her podis with prices, add her UPI code and send it to a WhatsApp broadcast list of her Sunday customers. It looks plain, almost embarrassing next to the shiny brands online. But on the first day, nine people order. She also applies for the basic food safety registration, because selling to strangers means taking that seriously. The website can wait.

ask.q: Customers want weekday orders. Karthik wants to build a full website first. What should Lakshmi do?
o: Start with a simple WhatsApp price card and learn from real orders
Build the full website so her brand looks professional from day one
Wait to take orders until she can afford a proper app
ask.why: The simplest version that lets real customers order starts the learning right away. A full website costs time and money before she knows what customers want online, and waiting for an app loses people who want to buy today. Rough is fine when it teaches.

chapters.take: Start with the simplest version real people can use, and improve from there.

story.b: Karthik posts a reel of Lakshmi roasting curry leaves in an iron kadai, and it spreads. In a week, her page has twelve hundred followers. The whole family is thrilled. But when Lakshmi checks her order notebook, the week looks almost like any other. Lots of hearts, very few rupees. So she starts tracking two different numbers. How many people order again within a month, and how many orders come from people who are not friends or relatives. These numbers are smaller and less exciting. But they tell her the truth. Customers who first bought a trial pack come back much more often than those who started with a big one. That is something she can act on.

ask.q: Lakshmi's reel brought twelve hundred followers but few new orders. Which numbers should guide her decisions?
o: Total followers, since a big audience will eventually buy
Repeat orders and orders from strangers, which show real buying
Likes on each post, to see which content is popular
ask.why: Followers and likes look exciting but do not tell her whether the business is working. Repeat orders and orders from strangers show real behaviour, and they reveal whether a change, like trial packs, actually helped. Vanity numbers can make her feel successful while sales stay flat.

chapters.take: Track numbers that show what people actually do, not just how popular you look.

story.b: At the end of the third month, Lakshmi sits down for her monthly check with the notebook and a cup of filter coffee. Local orders are steady but small. Then she notices something odd. Many of her biggest orders come from parents who ask her to pack the podis carefully so they can courier them to children studying or working in other cities. One mother has ordered four times, for her daughter in Pune. Lakshmi had never planned for these customers. She does not throw away her recipes or her Sunday stall. But she changes one key part of her plan, creating a sturdy home care parcel with three podis and a handwritten note, made for sending far away.

ask.q: Lakshmi notices her best customers are parents sending podi to children in other cities. What should she do?
o: Shift her focus toward these parcels while keeping what she has learned
Ignore it and keep pushing local sales, since that was the original plan
Start over with a completely new product like pickles
ask.why: When the evidence points somewhere new, changing one key part of the plan while keeping her recipes and lessons is smart learning. Sticking rigidly to the first plan ignores what customers are telling her. Starting over from zero throws away everything that already works.

chapters.take: Check regularly whether your plan is working. Pivot on evidence, not on panic.

story.h: Six months later in Saibaba Colony
story.b: Six months later, Lakshmi's kitchen has a second shelf just for courier boxes. Her home care parcels go to students and young workers in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi, packed by her and her neighbour Meena, whom she now pays. She still has her corner at Selvi's Sunday stall, where she tests every new flavour on real customers before making a big batch. Her notebook has a page for repeat orders, and she reads it every month. She never spent three lakh rupees. When Karthik suggests a website now, she agrees, because she finally knows exactly what it needs to do. Her late mother's idli podi is still the best seller.

chapters.take: Test small, learn fast and let real customers show you the way.
